input: In this worked example, we consider a flat firebrick wall with a thickness of 20 mm that separates two process streams, and our goal is to determine the steady heat flux passing through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the firebrick wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference that has been measured across the wall is 332 K, which is a substantial driving force for heat transfer. Under steady, one-dimensional conditions, the heat flux can be calculated by multiplying the thermal conductivity by the temperature difference and dividing the result by the wall thickness. Converting the thickness into metres gives us 0.02 m, and substituting the values into the expression gives the heat flux as 1.1 × 332 / 0.02 = 18260 W m-2. It is important to note that this figure is obtained on a conduction-only basis. The surface (film) resistances on either side of the wall have been excluded from the estimate, and if they were included, the flux would be lower, because the films would add further resistance in series with the wall itself and the temperature difference of 332 K would be shared across a greater total resistance. So the calculated value of 18260 W m-2 should be understood as the flux associated with the 20 mm firebrick wall on its own, under the measured temperature difference of 332 K, rather than as the flux that would necessarily be observed across the complete boundary between the two process streams.
target: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams, and the worked quantity is the steady heat flux through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. The measured temperature difference across the wall is 332 K. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is the conductivity multiplied by the temperature difference and divided by the thickness. The thickness in metres is 0.02 m, and substitution gives the heat flux as 1.1 × 332 / 0.02 = 18260 W m-2. The result is a conduction-only figure. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, because each film adds a resistance in series with the resistance of the wall, and the same temperature difference of 332 K would then be shared across wall and films together. The heat flux of 18260 W m-2 therefore belongs to the wall alone, across the full 20 mm of firebrick, under a temperature difference of 332 K applied across the wall itself. A flux for the wall as it stands between the two streams, films included, would be smaller, and the size of the reduction is set by film resistances that this example does not carry. The example closes on the wall value, and the wall value is the one its inputs determine.
